title: My Calendar III
statement:
Events arrive one at a time, and each event occupies the half-open time range `[startTime, endTime)`: it includes `startTime` but stops just before `endTime`. Say that `k` events form a *k-booking* when there is at least one moment that lies inside all `k` of them.

Implement the class `MyCalendarThree`:

- `MyCalendarThree()` creates a calendar with no events.
- `book(startTime, endTime)` always accepts the new event, adds it to the calendar, and returns the largest `k` for which some k-booking exists among all events booked so far (including this one).
constraints: At most 400 calls are made to book
notes:
## Intuition

Picture a counter that walks along the time line: it goes up by one when an event starts and down by one when an event ends. Its value at any moment is the number of events covering that moment, so the answer is the counter's peak. Only boundary times matter, because the count can change only there. Testing every event against every other event also works, but it is slower and easy to get wrong at touching ends.

## Approach

1. Keep `change`, a map from a boundary time to its net effect on the counter, and `times`, the same boundaries kept in sorted order.
2. In `book`, add `+1` at `startTime` and `-1` at `endTime` through `addBoundary`.
3. `addBoundary` inserts a new time into `times` at the position found by binary search, then adds `delta` to its entry in `change`.
4. Sweep `times` from left to right, adding each `change` to `active` and keeping the largest `active` in `best`. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

After `book(10, 20)` the boundaries are `10: +1, 20: -1`; the counter peaks at `1`. `book(50, 60)` adds a separate bump, still `1`. `book(10, 40)` makes `10: +2`, so the counter reaches `2` right at 10. `book(5, 15)` adds `5: +1, 15: -1`; the sweep reads 1 at 5, then 3 at 10: answer `3`. `book(5, 10)` gives `5: +2, 10: +1`, and the counter is 2 at 5 and still 3 at 10. `book(25, 55)` peaks at 2 near 25 and 50, so the answer stays `3`: `[null, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) per `book` with n events so far: the binary search is O(log n), but inserting into the array and the sweep are linear. O(n²) over all calls, tiny for 400 calls.
- Space: O(n) for the boundaries.

## Pitfalls

- The ranges are half-open: an event ending at 10 and one starting at 10 never overlap. Merging both into one net change at 10 handles this for free.
- Store net changes per time, not separate lists of starts and ends, or ties at the same time can be counted in the wrong order.
- The sweep must visit times in sorted order; a plain `Map` only remembers insertion order, which is why `times` exists.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `change` | net counter change at each boundary time |
| `times` | every boundary time, sorted |
| `active` | number of events covering the current point of the sweep |
| `best` | largest `active` seen in this sweep |
| `low`, `high`, `mid` | binary search bounds for the insert position |
| `delta` | `+1` for a start, `-1` for an end |
